chapter_title: Denial of Service (DoS) & Gas Limit Attacks

screens.title: Denial of Service (DoS) & Gas Limit Attacks
screens.subtitle: Why contract availability depends on gas-aware design

narration.text: In this lesson we will study how Denial of Service attacks appear in smart contracts and why Ethereum's gas model makes availability a design concern. You will learn what makes a function impossible to run, how unbounded loops and costly external dependencies lead to frozen features, and practical patterns—like pull-based payments and bounded batches—that restore scalability. We'll use concrete code examples to see a vulnerable push-style airdrop and then refactor it into a safe withdrawal-based design. Throughout, notice the trade-offs between simplicity and long-term availability: a neat push loop is easy to write but may become unusable when lists grow. Why this matters: a contract that can be locked by gas limits or by a paused dependency stops providing value and harms users. As you follow the examples, think about how you would test for edge cases with large datasets and how you would choose data structures or patterns to avoid single points of failure. By the end, you should be able to identify DoS risks in simple contracts and apply at least two mitigation strategies that keep your DApp usable.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Design contracts with gas and availability in mind: avoid unbounded work, prefer pull-based payments, bound iterations, and reduce reliance on single external points of failure.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide your practice: first, you'll define what a Denial of Service attack means for smart contracts, identifying how a contract can be prevented from performing its intended work. Second, you'll spot common patterns that invite DoS, including unbounded iterations and fragile external dependencies, and explain why gas limits matter. Third, you'll apply mitigation strategies such as pull-based payments, bounded iterations, and data structure redesign to keep contracts available and fair. Fourth, you'll evaluate third-party dependencies and ownership models to reduce single points of failure. Each objective pairs a clear skill with a reason it matters in production: availability protects users and preserves guarantees, mitigation patterns keep operations feasible as systems scale, and dependency scrutiny prevents DoS-by-proxy. We'll practice these skills with code refactors and testing steps that reinforce the ideas. By the end of the chapter you should be able to detect a DoS risk in a simple contract, propose at least two fixes, and design a basic test plan that simulates large datasets and gas pressure.

screens.title: What is DoS in smart contracts?
screens.subtitle: Define Denial of Service and how gas changes the threat model

narration.text: A Denial of Service attack in smart contracts stops legitimate users from getting the contract's intended behavior by making key operations fail or become prohibitively expensive. Unlike a traditional network DoS that floods bandwidth, smart-contract DoS typically targets computation and state on-chain by exploiting gas limits and cost semantics. A simple example is a function that must iterate over a growing list; as the list grows, required gas rises until the transaction exceeds the block gas limit and simply cannot be mined. Another example is making an essential call rely on an external contract that can be paused or manipulated, effectively denying service by proxy. Why this is important for you as a developer: contracts are immutable by default, and launching a contract that can be frozen breaks user expectations and can be exploited. Common misconceptions include thinking that only malicious actors cause DoS — in practice, normal growth of data can unintentionally cause the same effect if the design does not anticipate scale. In short, treat availability as a first-class requirement: quantify per-call gas, bound work, and prefer patterns that keep operations per-transaction predictable. A useful question to ask when reviewing a function is: could the gas cost grow without bound as on-chain state grows?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: DoS in smart contracts means making essential operations unusable by exhausting gas or relying on stoppable dependencies.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › What is DoS?
Definition

Denial of Service for smart contracts

A DoS on-chain prevents legitimate users from interacting with essential functions by making them fail or too expensive to run.

How it happens
  • Gas cost of an operation grows with state size until it exceeds the block gas limit.
  • External dependency can be paused or revert, blocking your contract's workflows.
  • An attacker can intentionally inflate state or spam costly functions to raise economic cost.
Common misconception
DoS is not always an explicit attack: unbounded growth or poor design can cause the same effect without a malicious actor.
Concrete example
Iterating over a growing array until gas exceeds block limit.
Imagine a reward function that loops through every participant. If participants reach thousands, the loop may never finish.
Key takeaway
Design for predictable per-transaction gas. If cost can grow without bound, refactor the pattern.

screens.title: Unbounded loop: VulnerableAirdrop walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Examine the push-style airdrop that can be DoS'd by scale

narration.text: Let's walk through a concrete vulnerable contract pattern: a push-style airdrop that iterates over an array of participants and transfers funds inside a loop. In this design, the distribution is a single transaction that tries to pay every participant. The core risk is that participants can grow without bound. As participants increase, the gas required to run the loop increases linearly and eventually surpasses the block gas limit, making the distribution function impossible to execute. Another subtle problem is that transferring funds inside a loop combines gas cost with external calls, which can also fail for one recipient and revert the whole transaction. A common misconception is that limiting per-transfer gas will help; in reality, the total gas required is the sum over all iterations and cannot be avoided by throttling single transfers. The concrete result: the contract's intended behavior—distributing funds—becomes unavailable. When auditing such code, ask how state grows and whether any operation depends on scanning full lists. Also check for external calls inside loops; they raise both reentrancy and availability concerns. In the next slide we will show a safer pattern that shifts cost to recipients.

keyIdea.title: Vulnerable pattern
keyIdea.text: A push-style loop that sends funds to every entry is fragile: growth in entries eventually makes the function uncallable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Unbounded loop: VulnerableAirdrop
Code walkthrough

VulnerableAirdrop

A single transaction tries to pay every participant. This scales poorly.

Key risks
  • Gas grows with participant count until it exceeds block limit.
  • External calls inside loops can revert and abort entire distribution.
  • Attackers can add junk entries to inflate cost.
Example code
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract VulnerableAirdrop {
  address[] public participants;
  mapping(address => bool) public hasReceivedAirdrop;

  function addParticipant(address _participant) public {
    participants.push(_participant);
  }

  // Vulnerable: Iterates over an unbounded array
  function distributeAirdrop(uint256 _amount) public {
    for (uint i = 0; i < participants.length; i++) {
      address participant = participants[i];
      if (!hasReceivedAirdrop[participant]) {
        (bool success, ) = participant.call{value: _amount}("");
        require(success, "Transfer failed");
        hasReceivedAirdrop[participant] = true;
      }
    }
  }
}
Concrete analogy
Think of a toll booth that must process every car in one minute. As cars grow, the single booth becomes a bottleneck and eventually cannot handle traffic.

screens.title: Pull-based payments (Withdrawal Pattern)
screens.subtitle: Shift cost to recipients to avoid DoS from distributions

narration.text: The pull-based payment pattern, also called the withdrawal pattern, avoids a single expensive distribution by letting recipients claim funds themselves. Instead of looping through every participant and pushing transfers, the contract records how much each participant can claim in a mapping. Each recipient then calls a withdraw function to receive their funds. This shifts gas costs to individual users and makes distribution scalable because each claim is limited in work and gas. Importantly, the withdraw function should follow the check-effects-interactions order: read the claimable amount, set it to zero, and then perform the external transfer. This reduces both DoS risk and reentrancy exposure. A common misunderstanding is that pull-based payments remove all operational costs — they do not; they redistribute cost so that no single transaction depends on the global set size. For applications where recipients are unwilling or unable to act, you can combine pull payments with incentives or a small relayer to help claims. In audits, verify that the mapping keys are correct, that balances are zeroed before transfer, and that there is no dependence on iterating other state during withdrawal.

keyIdea.title: Primary mitigation
keyIdea.text: Use pull-based payments: record claims per user and let recipients withdraw to avoid global loops and DoS.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Pull-based payments
Pattern

Withdrawal pattern

Record individual claims and let recipients pull funds to avoid large aggregate gas costs.

Benefits
  • Each transaction has bounded gas.
  • No single transaction depends on the number of recipients.
  • Reduces attack surface for DoS and reentrancy when done properly.
Misconception
Pull payments do not remove gas costs for users, but they prevent a single, unscalable operation.
Safe example
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SafeAirdrop {
  mapping(address => uint256) public claims;

  function recordClaim(address _participant, uint256 _amount) public {
    claims[_participant] += _amount;
  }

  // Safe: Each participant pulls their own funds
  function withdrawClaim() public {
    uint256 amount = claims[msg.sender];
    require(amount > 0, "No claimable funds");
    claims[msg.sender] = 0; // CEI: set balance to zero BEFORE transfer

    (bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{value: amount}("");
    require(success, "Transfer failed");
  }
}
Check your understanding
How would you help recipients who cannot pay gas to withdraw? Consider relayers or subsidized claims, but weigh centralization trade-offs.

screens.title: Bounded iteration and batching
screens.subtitle: Split work into safe, repeatable steps

narration.text: When iteration cannot be avoided, bounded processing is the pragmatic solution: process a limited number of elements per call and allow multiple calls to finish the job. Batching keeps each transaction's gas cost predictable and under the block gas limit. Implementations commonly accept start and end indices or a batch size parameter and enforce a maximum number of elements per invocation. When writing these functions, include guards that prevent out-of-bounds indexes and choose sensible batch caps based on expected gas per iteration. One subtle point: batching shifts complexity to callers or operators who must coordinate multiple calls to complete the work; make sure to document the required sequence and provide transparency on progress. A common mistake is to set an arbitrarily large batch size that still exceeds gas limits for some blocks; prefer conservative caps and let operators increase batch counts if needed. Batching also opens an opportunity for incentives: let anyone call the batch processor and reward them modestly, so maintenance does not rely on centralized actors. Overall, bounded iteration preserves availability while allowing large datasets to be processed safely.

keyIdea.title: Bounded processing
keyIdea.text: Process fixed-size batches per transaction so no single call needs unbounded gas; document and incentivize completion.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Bounded iteration & batching
Pattern

Batch processing

Accept a limited range or batch size and process only that set per call, keeping gas under control.

Implementation checklist
  • Validate bounds and batch size in require checks.
  • Keep per-item gas predictable and conservative.
  • Allow anyone to call batches and optionally provide a small reward.
Operational note
Track progress with indices or a queue so completions can be monitored and resumed safely.
Example
function distributeAirdropBatch(uint256 _startIndex, uint256 _endIndex, uint256 _amount) public {
  require(_endIndex < participants.length, "End index out of bounds");
  require(_endIndex - _startIndex <= 100, "Batch size too large (max 100)");

  for (uint i = _startIndex; i <= _endIndex; i++) {
    address participant = participants[i];
    // distribution logic
  }
}
Analogy
Process a fixed number of files at a time instead of trying to import everything in one run.

screens.title: Data structure redesign: arrays vs mappings vs Merkle trees
screens.subtitle: Choose the right storage approach for scalable claims

narration.text: Choosing the correct data structure on-chain has direct consequences for gas and availability. Dynamic arrays are convenient when you need enumeration, but they are a liability when operations iterate all entries. Mappings provide fast keyed access without an inherent enumerability cost; they are ideal for per-user balances or claimable amounts because they don't require scanning. For scenarios where you need off-chain lists with on-chain verification, Merkle trees are powerful: a root is stored on-chain and users present compact proofs to claim membership without storing the entire list. Each choice comes with trade-offs. Arrays simplify iteration and auditing but scale poorly. Mappings avoid iteration but do not let you list all keys on-chain; if you need listing, combine mapping storage with an off-chain index or events. Merkle proofs add complexity off-chain but keep on-chain storage minimal and gas predictable. When redesigning, ask whether you need on-chain enumeration or only validation. Also consider how an attacker might grow state: if anyone can push entries, prefer mappings and pull patterns. The right design minimizes per-transaction gas and avoids unbounded operations. Data structure redesign: arrays vs mappings vs Merkle trees means prefer mappings or merkle proofs for claim storage and avoid full enumeration on-chain unless strictly required.. In practical terms, choose the right storage approach for scalable claims. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design rule
keyIdea.text: Prefer mappings or Merkle proofs for claim storage and avoid full enumeration on-chain unless strictly required.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Data structure redesign
Arrays
Good for ordered lists and enumeration
Risk: iterating scales linearly and can exceed gas limits.
Mappings
Keyed access without enumeration cost
Use for claim balances and per-user flags to avoid full scans.
Merkle trees
Compact on-chain verification
Store a root and require off-chain proofs for membership to avoid on-chain lists.
Decision guide
  • If you need per-user claims without enumeration, prefer mappings.
  • If you must verify off-chain lists cheaply, use Merkle proofs.
  • If enumeration is required, combine arrays with batching and conservative caps.

screens.title: External contract dependencies and DoS-by-proxy
screens.subtitle: How third-party pauses or failures affect your DApp

narration.text: Contracts rarely exist in isolation. When your contract depends on external contracts—for tokens, oracles, or libraries—those dependencies become part of your attack surface. If an external token contract exposes a pause function or can be upgraded to revert certain operations, your contract's functionality can be interrupted even if your own code is correct. This is DoS by proxy. A classic example is relying on an ERC-20 implementation that the token owner can pause; if paused, transfers fail and dependent flows break. To mitigate this, carefully select dependencies with stable governance and track their invariants. Consider fallback paths: if a token is paused, you might support an alternate token or delay certain actions with transparent messaging. Use multi-sig and timelocks for your own critical controls so a single compromised key cannot halt your contract. A misconception is trusting that dependencies will always be available; in production, assume failure modes and design for graceful degradation. When auditing, map all external calls and consider what happens when each dependency stops responding or starts reverting. External contract dependencies and DoS-by-proxy means treat external contracts as potential points of failure and design fallbacks, redundancy, or safer interfaces to reduce dos risk by proxy.. In practical terms, how third-party pauses or failures affect your dapp. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Dependency principle
keyIdea.text: Treat external contracts as potential points of failure and design fallbacks, redundancy, or safer interfaces to reduce DoS risk by proxy.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › External contract dependencies
Risk

DoS by proxy

If an external contract can be paused, upgraded, or self-destructed, your contract may lose critical functionality.

Examples
  • An ERC-20 with a pause capability stops token transfers for your DApp.
  • An oracle contract that reverts or returns invalid data breaks dependent logic.
Mitigations
Use trusted providers, multiple oracle sources, fallback mechanisms, and decentralized governance for critical dependencies.
Concrete scenario
A paused token makes payment flows revert, which can prevent refunds or trades in your DApp and thus block users.
Checklist
Map external calls, document fallback behavior, and avoid critical flows that rely on a single dependency without redundancy.

screens.title: Gas limit attacks and economic DoS
screens.subtitle: When cost, not block limits, makes a function unusable

narration.text: Gas limit attacks are a related class where an attacker raises the economic cost of using a function until it is no longer feasible for honest users. Instead of necessarily exceeding block gas capacity, the attacker inflates storage or forces expensive calculations so that legitimate calls become prohibitively costly. For example, an attacker might spam junk data into a public mapping or repeatedly call a function that increases per-call work, driving up gas costs for everyone. Another technique is to trigger expensive computations in a function that any user must call, making the operation economically unattractive. The practical consequence is the same as classical DoS: the service becomes effectively unavailable. The difference is that the barrier is financial rather than purely technical. To mitigate this type of attack, design contracts to limit who can add costly data or add rate-limiting and quotas, and avoid placing expensive on-chain computations in publicly callable paths. When possible, move heavy computation off-chain or require a deposit to discourage spam. Always test for gas cost growth under adversarial inputs during audits and development. Gas limit attacks and economic DoS means an attacker can raise the cost of operations so users cannot afford to use them; mitigation includes limiting who can expand state and off-loading heavy computation off-chain.. In practical terms, when cost, not block limits, makes a function unusable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Economic DoS
keyIdea.text: An attacker can raise the cost of operations so users cannot afford to use them; mitigation includes limiting who can expand state and off-loading heavy computation off-chain.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Gas limit attacks
Threat

Economic Denial of Service

An attacker makes a function too expensive to call so honest users stop using it.

Examples
  • Spamming storage entries to inflate iteration costs.
  • Triggering heavy calculations on paths callable by anyone.
Mitigations
Restrict who can add costly data, use deposits to deter spam, off-load work off-chain or batch carefully.
Concrete exercise
Simulate an attacker adding many entries and measure gas growth for functions that process that state. Determine when the cost becomes unaffordable.
Pro-tip
Use gas profiling in test frameworks and run stress tests with adversarial scripts to reveal economic DoS vectors.

screens.title: Refactoring for DoS resistance: Starter code and steps
screens.subtitle: Guided refactor from push to pull payments

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through refactoring a vulnerable push-based payments contract into a safe pull-based system. Start by deploying the vulnerable contract and observing how paying all recipients in a single transaction can fail as the recipients array grows. The refactor steps are straightforward: stop storing a list for distribution; instead, when adding a recipient, record an individual claim amount in a mapping. Remove the bulk distribution function entirely and implement a withdraw function that zeros the claimant's balance before transferring funds. Remember the check-effects-interactions rule: update internal state first, then perform the external call. After refactoring, test with many recipients to confirm that no single transaction needs to process more than one claim. Also include a test that simulates malicious entries; for instance, try adding many recipients to observe distribution failure before the refactor and successful per-user claims after it. Finally, document the operational steps required if you still need a global migration or batch processing. This exercise will make the difference between a contract that fails silently at scale and one that continues to serve users reliably.

keyIdea.title: Refactor goal
keyIdea.text: Replace global push distributions with recorded claims and per-user withdrawals; test under scale to validate behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Refactor activity
Starter code
// VulnerablePaymentSystem (starter)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract VulnerablePaymentSystem {
  address[] public recipients;
  mapping(address => bool) public isRecipient;
  uint256 public paymentPerRecipient = 0.01 ether;

  function addRecipient(address _recipient) public {
    require(!isRecipient[_recipient], "Already a recipient");
    recipients.push(_recipient);
    isRecipient[_recipient] = true;
  }

  // Vulnerable to DoS if 'recipients' array grows too large
  function payAllRecipients() public payable {
    // owner guard omitted for brevity
    for (uint i = 0; i < recipients.length; i++) {
      address payable recipient = payable(recipients[i]);
      (bool success, ) = recipient.call{value: paymentPerRecipient}("");
      require(success, "Payment failed for a recipient");
    }
  }

  receive() external payable {}
}
Refactor steps
  1. Replace recipients array with mapping(address => uint256) claims.
  2. Record payable amounts via recordClaim instead of pushing to array.
  3. Implement withdraw that zeros balance before transfer.
  4. Test with increasing numbers of simulated recipients to confirm safety.
Testing tips
Use scripts to add thousands of recipients locally and run gas estimates on payAllRecipients before and after the refactor to see the difference.

screens.title: Common mistakes & defensive design checklist
screens.subtitle: Practical rules to avoid DoS and gas attacks

narration.text: When auditing or designing contracts, follow a defensive checklist to reduce DoS and gas risk. First, flag any unbounded loops or functions that depend on full enumeration; those need batching or redesign. Second, identify external calls inside loops and treat them as both DoS and reentrancy risks. Third, review ownership and control flows: a single owner who can pause or kill the contract introduces a central point that, if compromised, creates DoS. Fourth, evaluate external dependencies and prefer redundant or decentralized providers for critical services. Fifth, measure gas consumption under expected and adversarial state sizes, not just happy-path tests. Sixth, prefer pull-based payments and mappings for per-user balances; use Merkle proofs where appropriate. Seventh, document operational procedures for batch processors and consider incentive mechanisms for public callers that maintain the contract. Finally, incorporate multi-sig, time-locks, and explicit upgrade paths where necessary to balance availability with governance. These defensive practices form a checklist you can apply during design reviews, code audits, and testing. Common mistakes & defensive design checklist means audit for unbounded work, external calls in loops, single points of control, and test gas under stress; prefer pull payments and bounded batches.. In practical terms, practical rules to avoid dos and gas attacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Checklist
keyIdea.text: Audit for unbounded work, external calls in loops, single points of control, and test gas under stress; prefer pull payments and bounded batches.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Defensive checklist
Audit flags
  • Unbounded loops over on-chain arrays.
  • External calls inside iteration.
  • Single-owner pause or kill controls.
Design rules
  • Prefer pull-based payments and mappings.
  • Use batching with conservative caps if iteration needed.
  • Consider Merkle proofs for large, verifiable lists.
Operational steps
  • Stress test with large datasets and adversarial inputs.
  • Document batch progress and provide relayers or incentives.
  • Use multi-sig and time-locks for critical controls.
Key takeaway
View availability as an engineering constraint. Design, test, and document for scale and adversarial behavior.

screens.title: Testing for DoS and gas exhaustion
screens.subtitle: Plan tests that reveal scalability and dependency failures

narration.text: Testing for DoS involves two complementary approaches: scale testing and adversarial testing. Scale testing simulates expected growth by populating contracts with many entries and running gas estimations on key functions. This reveals whether operations will eventually exceed block limits. Adversarial testing simulates an attacker who intentionally inflates state with junk data, calls expensive functions repeatedly, or manipulates external dependencies to pause or revert. Include unit tests that assert gas usage stays below conservative thresholds for a variety of dataset sizes, and run integration tests that simulate external dependencies failing. Use local forks or testnets to measure real gas usage and run stress scripts that call functions many times to model realistic pressure. Remember to test both functional correctness and operational behavior: for instance, verify that after a refactor to pull payments, individual withdrawals still complete successfully even when other users' state is large or malicious. Finally, include monitoring and alerts in production to detect runaway growth in state or unexpected gas spikes so you can respond before users are affected. Testing for DoS and gas exhaustion means combine large-scale state tests with adversarial simulations and dependency failure scenarios; monitor production for growth and gas spikes.. In practical terms, plan tests that reveal scalability and dependency failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test plan
keyIdea.text: Combine large-scale state tests with adversarial simulations and dependency failure scenarios; monitor production for growth and gas spikes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Testing & Validation
Scale tests
Populate large arrays or maps and measure gas per operation across dataset sizes.
Adversarial tests
Simulate spam entries, repeated expensive calls, and dependency pauses to observe behavior.
Integration tests
Fork mainnet or use testnets to measure real gas and confirm behavior with actual dependency contracts.
Monitoring
Set alerts for rapid state growth and unusually high gas per transaction so you can investigate early.

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts you must keep in mind. First, Denial of Service in smart contracts means making a contract's operations unusable, often by exhausting gas or using stoppable dependencies. Second, the Block Gas Limit caps how much computation can be included in a single block, and this makes unbounded loops especially dangerous. Third, an Unbounded Loop is any loop that can grow with on-chain state to the point that its gas cost becomes infeasible. These three ideas form the conceptual foundation: if you can map a function to one of these risks, you know to redesign or add constraints. Keep these terms handy when you read code or write tests, and use them as a checklist during design reviews. Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Key Concepts — Part 1
Denial of Service (DoS)
An attack or failure that prevents users from accessing contract behavior.
Block Gas Limit
The maximum gas that all transactions in a block can consume; operations must fit beneath it.
Unbounded Loop
A loop over state that can grow arbitrarily, risking gas exhaustion and DoS.
Summary takeaway

Use these concepts as a rapid triage: if a function iterates over state or relies on a stoppable dependency, treat it as high risk and apply pull, batch, or redesign patterns.

narration.text: Now review the core mitigation concepts you will apply. Pull-based Payments move the cost of distribution from the contract to recipients, avoiding large global transactions. Bounded Iteration means processing fixed-size batches so each transaction stays within gas limits. External Contract Dependencies refer to any third-party contracts your code calls; treat them as potential failure points and design fallbacks. Together these ideas form practical controls: shift cost when possible, limit per-call work, and reduce reliance on single providers. When you combine them with testing and operational monitoring, you create contracts that remain usable as they scale and under adversarial conditions.
